title: Periodic Properties and Variations
tagline: How atomic size, energy and character change across periods and down groups — and why the pattern repeats.

overview.intro: The periodic table is not a poster of elements; it is a map of behaviour. Once an element is placed, its size, energy and character follow from that placement. This chapter takes the trends one property at a time, states the reason behind each one in plain words, and then puts them together so that a single glance at a group or a period tells you what an element will do in a reaction. Board questions in this unit nearly always ask for the trend, the reason behind it, and one example.

facts.label: Modern periodic law
facts.value: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

facts.label: Long form table
facts.value: 18 groups and 7 periods, arranged by increasing atomic number.

facts.label: What repeats
facts.value: Similar valence electron arrangement gives similar chemical behaviour.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: One compulsory short-answer set plus a choice of longer trend questions.

learningOutcomes: State the modern periodic law and explain why atomic number replaced atomic mass as the basis of classification.
Predict the direction of change of atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity across a period and down a group, with a reason for each.
Distinguish metallic and non-metallic character and use them to identify metals, non-metals and metalloids on the table.
Explain the anomalies of the second and third periods and use trends to compare named pairs of elements.
Use valence shell configuration to place an element in its group and period and to suggest its likely charge in compounds.

learn.title: Building the table: from Mendeleev to the modern form

blocks.text: Mendeleev arranged the known elements in order of atomic mass and found that elements with similar properties recurred at regular intervals, so he left gaps for elements he had not yet discovered and even predicted their properties. The modern table keeps that repeating idea but uses atomic number as the sorting key. The modern periodic law states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. Because atomic number counts protons in the nucleus, it fixes the electron arrangement, and the electron arrangement decides chemical behaviour. The result is 18 groups standing for the number of valence electrons or a shared outer-shell pattern, and 7 periods standing for the number of occupied shells.

items: Groups run vertically: elements in one group share the same number of valence electrons and so show similar compound formulas and reactions.
Periods run horizontally: the number of shells stays the same across a period while the nuclear charge increases, which pulls the electrons in more tightly.
Blocks s, p, d and f mark which sub-shell is being filled; the transition elements fill the d sub-shell inside period 4 and beyond.
Valence, shown at the top of most tables, gives the usual combining capacity and links directly to the charge an ion carries.

items.meaning: Number of protons in the nucleus; it defines the element and fixes its position in the table.
Electrons in the outermost shell, the ones that take part in bonding and decide the group.
A horizontal row; its number equals the number of occupied electron shells in a neutral atom.
The regular recurrence of similar properties as atomic number increases.

blocks.text: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together. Across a period the number of shells does not change but the number of protons rises, so the effective nuclear charge pulls the outer shell closer and the atom shrinks. Down a group each element adds a whole new shell, and that extra shell outweighs the extra protons, so the atom grows. The same reasoning explains ions: a cation is smaller than its parent atom because it has lost a shell or lost the repulsion of the removed electron, while an anion is larger because the same nucleus now holds more electrons and they push each other apart.

items: Across a period, left to right: atomic radius decreases steadily, with the noble gas measured differently because it does not form normal bonds.
Down a group, top to bottom: atomic radius increases because each step adds a complete electron shell.
Isoelectronic species, those with the same number of electrons, shrink as the nuclear charge rises: N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+, Al3+ in that order of decreasing size.
Cations are smaller than the parent atom; anions are larger than the parent atom.

items.note: Losing the whole third shell makes the ion much smaller than the atom.
The same 17 protons now hold 18 electrons, so the cloud spreads out.

learn.title: Ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity

blocks.text: Three energy measures describe how greedily an atom holds electrons. Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms. Electron affinity is the energy released when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms. Electronegativity is the ability of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair towards itself. All three follow the same logic as size: small atoms hold their electrons tightly, so removal costs more and addition releases more, while large atoms with distant outer electrons hold them loosely.

items: Ionisation energy increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Electron affinity is generally most negative (most energy released) among the halogens, because a nearly full shell completes itself.
Electronegativity peaks at fluorine, the smallest and most electronegative element, and falls as size grows.
A full shell or a half-filled sub-shell is unusually stable, so elements such as nitrogen, with a half-filled 2p sub-shell, give higher ionisation energies than their neighbours.
Write the two energy processes as equations with state symbols, because the symbols carry marks: Na(g) → Na+(g) + e- for ionisation energy, Cl(g) + e- → Cl-(g) for electron affinity.
Oxide character follows the same trend: Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH gives a basic solution, while Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O and Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O show its amphoteric nature.

items.text: Removing an electron from Na costs relatively little
items.note: Na has one loosely held 3s electron and becomes the stable Na+ configuration.

items.text: Cl releases the most energy when it gains an electron
items.note: Seven valence electrons plus one completes the octet to reach Ar-like arrangement.

blocks.caption: Trend summary for period 3
rows: More protons, same number of shells
Harder to pull an electron from a smaller, more positive atom
Smaller bonded atom attracts the shared pair more strongly
Atoms hold their own electrons less readily available to lose

blocks.text: Metallic character is the readiness to lose electrons and form cations; non-metallic character is the readiness to gain electrons or attract shared pairs. Metals sit on the left and centre of the table, non-metals on the upper right, and the staircase of metalloids separates them. Metallic character therefore falls across a period, because atoms hold their electrons more tightly, and rises down a group, because the outer electrons are further from the nucleus. Reactivity of metals follows the ease of losing an electron, so the most reactive metals are the bottom of group 1, while the most reactive non-metals are the top of group 17.

items: Group 1 alkali metals react vigorously with water and become more violent down the group as ionisation energy falls.
Group 17 halogens react by gaining an electron and become less reactive down the group as size grows and affinity falls.
Noble gases hold a complete octet, so they are neither metallic nor non-metallic in behaviour and rarely form compounds.
Metalloids such as silicon and germanium lie along the staircase and show intermediate, semi-conducting behaviour.
Reactivity of group 1 can be written as an equation: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2, with potassium reacting faster because its valence electron is held less tightly.
Halogen displacement gives the group trend in one line: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2, a reaction that becomes less vigorous down the group.

items.text: Potassium fizzes on water while lithium reacts steadily
items.note: Down group 1, ionisation energy falls, so the metal gives up its electron faster.

items.text: Fluorine attacks almost everything while iodine reacts sluggishly
items.note: Up group 17, the atom is smaller and attracts an incoming electron more strongly.

items.meaning: Tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions; increases down a group and decreases across a period.
Tendency to gain electrons or attract shared pairs; increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Element along the staircase of the table, such as silicon, with properties between metals and non-metals.

learn.title: Using trends: comparisons, anomalies and exam-style reasoning

blocks.text: Most exam answers in this unit have three parts: the trend, the reason, and a named example. Write the trend first as one sentence, then give the reason in terms of shells versus nuclear charge, then quote a pair of elements as evidence. The second and third periods give the famous anomalies. Lithium is larger than expected because it has only two shells and a small nucleus; beryllium is smaller than expected relative to lithium; boron is smaller still, while nitrogen, with a half-filled 2p sub-shell, resists losing an electron better than oxygen does. Recognising these exceptions earns the extra mark that a plain trend statement cannot.

items: Always compare like with like: two atoms, two ions, or two tendencies in the same direction of the table.
Quote the electron arrangement when you explain a size difference; it proves the shells argument.
For an anomaly, name the special stability: full shell, half-filled sub-shell or an extra repulsion between paired electrons.
Practice the standard pairs: O and S, Na and K, F and Cl, N and O, Mg and Ca.

items.text: Why is the ionisation energy of nitrogen higher than that of oxygen?
items.note: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell that is extra stable; oxygen must remove one of four 2p electrons, where electron-electron repulsion eases removal.

items.text: Why does fluorine have the highest electronegativity?
items.note: It is the smallest halogen, so its nucleus holds the shared pair at the shortest distance with the least shielding.

keyPoints: The modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic mass.
Group number gives valence electrons for s and p block elements; period number gives the number of occupied shells.
Atomic radius decreases across a period (same shells, more protons) and increases down a group (new shell added).
Ionisation energy increases across a period and decreases down a group, because removal gets harder as size falls.
Electron affinity is most energy-releasing for the halogens; electronegativity is highest for fluorine.
Metallic character means readiness to lose electrons; it falls across a period and grows down a group.
Isoelectronic ions shrink as nuclear charge rises: N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+ > Al3+.
Cations are smaller than their atoms, anions larger, because shells are lost or electron repulsion grows.
Half-filled and fully filled sub-shells are extra stable and produce anomalies such as nitrogen against oxygen.
Reactivity of metals follows ease of electron loss; reactivity of non-metals follows ease of electron gain.
examFocus: Define the modern periodic law in one sentence, then give the two consequences: fixed group for similar valence and periodic repetition.
A trend question wants three parts every time: state the trend, explain it using shells against nuclear charge, and name one example pair.
Anomalies earn marks: learn nitrogen versus oxygen in ionisation energy and lithium versus beryllium in size.
For ion diagrams, draw the parent atom and the ion with the correct electron arrangement before writing the comparison.

vocabulary.meaning: Regular repetition of similar properties as atomic number increases.
Energy required to remove one electron from one gaseous atom.
Energy released when one electron is added to one gaseous atom.
Ability of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair of electrons.
Species having the same number of electrons, such as O2- and F-.
Reduction of the effective nuclear pull on outer electrons by inner shells.
The outermost occupied electron shell, which takes part in bonding.
Element with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, along the staircase.

questions.prompt: The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing:
questions.explanation: The modern periodic law sorts elements by atomic number, which counts protons and fixes the electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which property increases steadily across a period from left to right?
questions.explanation: Nuclear charge rises with the same number of shells, so removing an electron needs more energy.

questions.prompt: Among the isoelectronic species N3-, O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+, the largest is:
questions.explanation: All five have 10 electrons, so the one with the fewest protons holds them least tightly and is largest.

questions.prompt: The ionisation energy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen mainly because:
options: Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p sub-shell
Nitrogen has a higher atomic number
questions.answer: Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p sub-shell
questions.explanation: A half-filled 2p3 arrangement is extra stable; in oxygen a paired 2p electron is easier to remove.

questions.prompt: The horizontal rows of the periodic table are called __________ and their number equals the number of occupied electron shells.
questions.explanation: A period is a horizontal row; the period number counts the shells a neutral atom occupies.

questions.prompt: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms is called __________ energy.
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy is measured for gaseous atoms so that no intermolecular forces interfere.

questions.answer: Properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
questions.explanation: As atomic number increases by one, properties change regularly and repeat at fixed intervals, giving the groups.
questions.commonMistake: Do not write Mendeleev’s mass-based law; the modern law names atomic number.

questions.prompt: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period even though electrons are being added?
questions.answer: Because each added electron enters the same shell while protons are added to the nucleus, so the effective nuclear pull on the outer shell increases and the atom contracts.
questions.explanation: The shell count stays constant across a period, so extra nuclear charge wins over the small increase in electron repulsion.

questions.prompt: Arrange the ions N3-, O2-, F- and Na+ in decreasing order of ionic size and give one reason.
questions.answer: N3- > O2- > F- > Na+; they are isoelectronic, so the ion with the fewest protons attracts its electrons least strongly and is largest.
questions.explanation: All four hold 10 electrons, so nuclear charge alone decides the size order.

questions.prompt: Explain with reasons why ionisation energy increases from sodium to chlorine.
questions.answer: Across period 3 both elements have three shells, but chlorine has 17 protons against sodium’s 11. The larger effective nuclear charge holds the outer electrons closer and more tightly, so progressively more energy is needed to remove one. The values rise steadily from sodium, which loses its single 3s electron easily, to chlorine, which strongly retains seven 3p electrons.
questions.explanation: Shell count is constant while nuclear charge rises, so attraction to the outer shell strengthens across the period.

questions.prompt: Describe how metallic character varies in the periodic table and relate it to reactivity of group 1 metals.
questions.answer: Metallic character, the readiness to lose electrons, decreases across a period because rising nuclear charge holds electrons more tightly, and increases down a group because added shells place the valence electron further from the nucleus. For group 1 this means reactivity rises down the group: lithium reacts steadily with water, while potassium reacts violently, because the outer electron is held less tightly and is lost sooner.
questions.explanation: Ease of electron loss governs metallic character, and that ease grows as the outer shell moves further out.

questions.prompt: An element X has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 7. Identify its group and period, state whether it is a metal or a non-metal, and predict the charge of its ion.
questions.answer: X has three shells, so it is in period 3; it has seven valence electrons, so it is in group 17, the halogens. Being on the upper right of the staircase it is a non-metal, and it gains one electron to complete its octet, forming the X- ion with a single negative charge.
questions.explanation: Seven valence electrons means gaining one rather than losing seven, which is exactly the halogen pattern.
